en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Puzzles, Section on the Power of Supernatural Faculties (Iddhibalavagga)
2. The Question on Omniscience “Venerable Nāgasena, is the Buddha omniscient?

“Yes, Great King, the Blessed One is omniscient; yet the Blessed One’s knowledge and vision are not constantly and continuously present before him. The Blessed One’s knowledge of omniscience is dependent upon advertence; having adverted, he knows whatever he wishes.”
“Therefore, venerable Nāgasena, the Buddha is not omniscient,
if his omniscient knowledge comes about through seeking.
“Great King, there are one hundred cartloads of rice, and thirty-seven and a half cartloads of rice, and two measures of rice.”
If one were to set up a hundred thousand measures of paddy, would they be exhausted and depleted by the thoughts occurring in the space of a single finger-snap?
In this regard, seven types of thoughts occur:

those thoughts, O Great King, of those who possess lust, hatred, and delusion; who possess defilements; whose bodies are uncultivated, whose virtue is uncultivated, whose minds are uncultivated, and whose wisdom is uncultivated—their thought arises with heaviness and proceeds sluggishly.
For what reason?
Because of the lack of cultivation of the mind.

Great King, just as when a bamboo pole is spread out, made wide and broad, interlaced and intertwined, and entangled with a mass of branches, its progress is heavy and its coming is slow when it is being pulled along.
For what reason?
Because the branches are intertwined and entangled.

In the same way, Great King, for those who possess lust, hatred, and delusion, who are possessed of defilements, and who have not cultivated the body, virtue, mind, or wisdom, their consciousness arises with heaviness and proceeds sluggishly.
For what reason?
Because it is interwoven and entangled with defilements; this is the first consciousness.
Now, this second consciousness enters into analysis:

“Great King, as for those stream-enterers who have closed off the states of misery, attained right view, and understood the Teacher’s instruction—their consciousness arises lightly and proceeds lightly in three respects;
it arises heavily and proceeds sluggishly in the higher planes.
For what reason?”
Because the mind is purified in three places, yet the defilements above them have not been abandoned.

Great King, it is just as when a bamboo stalk has its three joints thoroughly cleared, but the upper part is entangled with a mass of branches; when one pulls it, it moves easily as far as the three joints, but from there upwards it is stiff.
For what reason?
Because it is pure at the base and because its branches are entangled with one another above.
In the same way, Great King, for those stream-enterers who have closed off the states of woe, attained right view, and understood the Teacher’s instruction,
their mind arises lightly and proceeds lightly in three respects, but it is heavy in the higher stages.
It arises slowly and proceeds sluggishly.
For what reason?
Because the mind is purified in three respects but the defilements above those have not yet been abandoned; this is the second type of consciousness.
In this regard, O Great King, this third state of mind is analyzed as follows:

those who are once-returners, whose lust, hatred, and delusion have been attenuated—their minds arise lightly and proceed lightly in five respects, but they arise heavily and proceed sluggishly in the higher planes.
For what reason?
Because the mind is purified in five places, yet the defilements above them have not been abandoned.

Great King, it is just as when a bamboo stalk is pure in its five joints but entangled above by a mass of branches: when it is being pulled, it moves easily as far as the five joints, but above that it is stiff.
For what reason?
Because it is pure below and because its branches are entangled with a dense thicket above.
In the same way, Great King, for those once-returners whose lust, hatred, and delusion have become attenuated,
their mind arises lightly and proceeds lightly regarding the five lower stages, but it is heavy regarding the higher planes.
It arises slowly and proceeds sluggishly.
Why? Because the mind is purified in five respects but the higher defilements have not yet been abandoned; this is the third type of consciousness.
In this regard, this is the fourth way the mind is analyzed:
O Great King, for those non-returners who have abandoned the five lower fetters,
their mind arises lightly and proceeds lightly in ten respects, but it arises heavily and proceeds slowly in the higher planes.
For what reason?
Because the mind is purified in ten stages, yet the defilements above those have not been abandoned.

Great King, it is just as when a bamboo stalk has been cleared of the knots at its ten sections, but above that remains entangled with a mass of branches; when it is being pulled upward, it moves easily as far as the tenth section, but from there on it becomes stiff.
For what reason?
Because it is pure at the base and because its branches are entangled with one another above.
In the same way, Great King, those who are non-returners (anāgāmin) have abandoned the five lower fetters (pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni).
Their mind arises lightly and proceeds lightly in ten instances,
but it arises heavily and proceeds sluggishly in the higher planes.
For what reason?
Because the mind is purified in ten respects, yet higher defilements have not yet been abandoned, this is the fourth state of consciousness.
Herein, this fifth state of consciousness is explained:

"Those, O Great King, who are Arahants with taints destroyed, whose impurities are washed away, who have vomited out the defilements, who have lived the holy life, and who have done what was to be done."
For those who have laid down the burden, achieved their own goal, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, attained the analytical knowledges, and are purified in the stages of disciples,
that mind arises quickly and proceeds quickly within the domain of disciples; but within the stages of paccekabuddhas,
it arises slowly and proceeds sluggishly.
For what reason?
Because the domain of the disciples is pure, whereas the domain of the paccekabuddhas is impure.
Great King, it is just as when a bamboo pole, being entirely free from all knots and joints, moves with lightness and without delay when being pulled.
For what reason?
Because the entire bamboo-joint is purified and free from entanglement.
In the same way, Great King, those who are Arahants, whose taints are exhausted, whose impurities are washed away, whose defilements have been vomited out, and who have lived the holy life...
For those who have done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and reached the analytical knowledges—
being utterly purified on the plane of disciples— their mind arises quickly and proceeds quickly within the domain of disciples;
yet it arises slowly and proceeds sluggishly on the plane of Paccekabuddhas.
For what reason?
Because it is pure within the domain of the disciples, yet impure within the domain of the paccekabuddhas; this is the fifth consciousness.
Herein, this sixth consciousness is now being analyzed:
"Great King, those Paccekabuddhas who are self-become, teacherless, solitary wanderers like the horn of a rhinoceros,
whose minds are pure and stainless within their own domain— their mind arises lightly and functions lightly within their own domain,
but it arises heavily and functions sluggishly regarding the stages of an omniscient Buddha."
For what reason?
Because his own domain is pure and the domain of the omniscient Buddha is vast.
Great King, it is just as if a man were to cross a small river in his own domain, day or night, at will and without fear.
Suppose he were to step down, and then, seeing further on the great ocean— deep, vast, bottomless, and shoreless—
he were to become afraid, hesitate, and be unable to step down.
For what reason?
Because he has crossed over his own domain and because of the vastness of the great ocean.
In the same way, Great King, as for those Paccekabuddhas who are self-become, without a teacher, wandering alone like the horn of a rhinoceros,
whose minds are pure and stainless within their own domain— their mind arises lightly within their own domain, very lightly.
It proceeds, but it arises with weight and proceeds slowly on the levels of the omniscient Buddhas.
For what reason?
Because of its utter purity and because the domain of an omniscient Buddha is vast within its own sphere; this is the sixth consciousness.
In this regard, O Great King, this seventh mind comes to be analyzed as follows:
the minds of those Perfectly Enlightened Ones— who are omniscient, possessors of the ten powers, confident in the four grounds of self-confidence,
endowed with the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, infinite victors, and possessed of unobstructed knowledge— are light in every respect.
It arises lightly and proceeds smoothly.
For what reason?
Because it is completely purified in every respect.
“Great King, would there be any hesitation or sticking when a well-polished, stainless, unencumbered arrow with a fine tip—
straight, unbent, and not crooked— is released from a strong bow and struck against fine linen, fine cotton, or fine wool?”
“No indeed, venerable sir.
“For what reason?
“Because of the fineness of the garments, their being well-washed, and the force of the arrow’s impact.”
In the same way, Great King, the minds of those Perfectly Enlightened Ones— who are omniscient, possessors of the ten powers, confident in the four grounds of self-confidence,
endowed with the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, infinite victors, and possessed of unobstructed knowledge—
arise lightly in all respects and proceed lightly.
What is the reason?
Because it is completely purified in every respect; this is the seventh consciousness.

In this regard, Great King, that which is the consciousness of the omniscient Buddhas transcends the calculation of even those six types of consciousness, being purified and light through incalculable qualities.
And because the Blessed One’s mind is both completely pure and light, therefore, Great King, the Blessed One displays the Twin Miracle.
Regarding the Twin Miracle, Great King, it should be understood that the minds of the Blessed Buddhas revolve so swiftly;
there is no further reason to be stated in this matter. Moreover, Great King, those miracles belong to the omniscient Buddhas.
Compared to the mind, even counting, calculation, reckoning, or even a fraction of a reckoning do not approach it;
for the Blessed One’s omniscient knowledge, O Great King, is dependent upon advertence (*āvajjana*). Having adverted, he knows whatever he desires.
Just as, O Great King, a man might place whatever is held in one hand into the other with an open palm.
One might utter speech with the mouth, swallow food that has entered the mouth, open the eyes after closing them, or close the eyes after opening them;
one might extend an arm that was contracted, or contract an arm that was extended.
Great King, this is more sluggish than the Blessed One’s omniscient knowledge, more sluggish than his act of adverting; for having adverted—
“He knows whatever he wishes; it is not on account of a mere lack of advertence that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are called non-omniscient.
“Even advertence, venerable Nāgasena, must be performed through seeking; please, sir, convince me in this matter with a reason.
“Just as, great king, for a man who is wealthy, of great riches, of great possessions, and possessed of abundant gold and silver...”

Suppose there were abundant wealth and resources, abundant money and grain— rice, paddy, barley, husked rice, sesame, mung beans, black gram, food for the morning, and food for the evening— as well as ghee, oil, fresh butter, milk, curd, honey, molasses,
and treacle, all contained in granaries, jars, pots, and storehouses;
and suppose a guest were to arrive at that man’s house, one worthy of hospitality and desiring a meal, yet whatever cooked food was in his house had already been finished.
“Suppose, Kumbhita, one were to take rice out [of a granary] and cook it for a meal;
even so, Great King, would that person be called poor or wretched merely because of that slight deficiency of food?
“No indeed, Bhante. Even in the house of a wheel-turning monarch, Bhante, there is no lack of food at the wrong time; how much less so in the case of a householder?”
“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata’s omniscient knowledge lacks only the act of attention; having directed his attention, he knows whatever he wishes.
Or again, Great King, suppose there were a tree laden with fruit, bent down and bowed under the weight of its clusters;
would there be any fruit that had not fallen from it? Would that tree, Great King, by the mere deficiency of such fallen fruit, [be considered lacking]?”
“Would it not be fruitless?
“No, venerable sir; those fruits of the tree are dependent upon falling. Once they have fallen, one may take them as one wishes.
“In the same way, great king, the Tathāgata’s omniscient knowledge is dependent upon his attention. Having directed his attention, he knows whatever he wishes.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, does the Buddha know whatever he wishes to know by repeatedly attending to it?
“Yes, Great King, the Blessed One knows whatever he wishes to know by repeatedly attending to it.
Just as, Great King, when a Wheel-turning Monarch calls to mind the Wheel-treasure, saying, ‘Let the Wheel-treasure come to me,’ and having been called to mind, the Wheel-treasure comes;”
“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata, having repeatedly directed his attention, knows whatever he wishes.
“Firm is the reason, venerable Nāgasena; the Buddha is omniscient. We accept that the Buddha is omniscient.
The second dilemma: on the omniscience of the Buddha.
